Heidegger’s analysis of temporality as ecstatic, futural, hermeneutic and non-absolute supplies the explicit analytic that Pannenberg uses to universalise historicity. What Heidegger describes for Dasein’s being-towards-death is read by Pannenberg as the structure of being as such, so that human history is no longer ontologically privileged over the history of the cosmos. It is this Heideggerian de-anthropologisation of time that makes the eschewal of artificial distinctions between types of history possible.

Schelling’s Naturphilosophie is background context for thinking nature as process, but the operative conceptual work on time, contingency and the dissolution of the human/natural history divide in the physics-engaged, late work is carried by Scotus for the modal contingency of time and Heidegger for its ecstatic, historically disclosed structure. That is the Scotist-Heideggerian pairing that underwrites Pannenberg’s model of a cosmic history built on a contingent concept of time.

What changes is the anthropocentric boundary around “history” is removed, and that removal requires both a metaphysics of contingency and a phenomenology of temporality.

The metaphysics of contingency is Scotist and it is unanimous. The case for a time that can be genuinely historical in the cosmic sense, i.e. a time that is not a necessary, eternalist container, is Pannenberg’s retrieval of John Duns Scotus against the Augustinian-Thomist necessity of time. Scotus’ doctrine of the absolute contingency of creation, the primacy of potentia and the openness of the future gives Pannenberg the theological grammar for a world whose temporal order is free and could have been otherwise, and therefore for a history that is not teleologically necessitated. That is the Scotist ground for the contingent concept of time the question names.

What is needed second is the description of that contingent time as a horizon, not a container, and the dissolution of the modern partition between natural and human kinds of history. That is where Martin Heidegger is decisive for Pannenberg, not Schelling as a primary temporal partner.

Pannenberg takes up Heidegger’s existential analytic of temporality in Being and Time, the deconstruction of metaphysical time as absolute presence-at-hand, and the ecstatic, futural, hermeneutic structure of temporality, and he transposes it cosmologically. Once time is understood as ecstatic and historically disclosed rather than as Newtonian absolute succession, the artificial distinction between “natural history” and “human history” collapses: both are expressions of one contingent becoming. Heidegger gives Pannenberg the means to say that human history has no intrinsic ontological privilege over the history of the cosmos, and to read the relational, non-absolute time disclosed by modern physics theologically.

Schelling’s Naturphilosophie is certainly in the background as a resource for thinking nature as process and for the Idea of a non-anthropocentric cosmic process, and it is often cited alongside Pannenberg. But it is not the primary articulation of the contingent concept of time itself. The explicit philosophical work on time as contingent, relational and future-open, the work that lets Pannenberg re-interpret history without abandoning it and to model cosmic history on a contingent temporality, is carried by Scotus for the modal ontology and Heidegger for the phenomenological-ontological description of temporality.

That pairing underwrites the claim that there is no real reason to hold human history as of more cosmic interest than other histories, and that the reinterpreted history is a single, contingent cosmic history whose meaning is eschatologically open.

Heidegger supplies that description. Pannenberg takes up the analysis of temporality in Being and Time as ecstatic, finite and futural, time as the horizon of historicity rather than an absolute container. Human history becomes a particular instance of a more primordial cosmic temporality, and there is no principled reason to privilege it over the history of the cosmos as a whole.

Y. John Duns Scotus and Martin Heidegger

Pannenberg’s late cosmic re-reading is presented as a continuation, not an abandonment, of his earlier theology of history. The re-description is made possible by keeping the historicity claim but re-grounding it in a contingent, open temporality that can be shared by nature and spirit.

The metaphysical warrant for that contingency is Scotist. Pannenberg repeatedly retrieves John Duns Scotus against the Augustinian-Thomist necessitarian picture of time: creation and time are radically contingent, the world is not a necessary emanation of the divine essence, and the future is formally open. That Scotist doctrine of the contingency of being and of the beginning of time with creation supplies the theological grammar for a time that is not absolute, necessary or teleologically closed, and for a cosmic history that is genuinely open to an eschatological future rather than logically necessitated.

The phenomenological description of that time is Heideggerian. Pannenberg takes up Heidegger’s analysis of temporality in *Sein und Zeit* – time as ecstatic, future-directed, finite and the horizon of historicity – and transposes it from Dasein to being as such. Once time is understood as ecstatic-historical rather than as a neutral Newtonian container, the modern artificial partition between “natural history” and “human history” dissolves. Human history is one instance of a more primordial cosmic temporality; there is no intrinsic ontological reason to privilege human history over the history of the cosmos.

Hence the contingent concept of time is Scotist in its modal foundation and Heideggerian in its temporal articulation. Together they let Pannenberg eschew the artificial distinctions between types of history and defend a single, contingent cosmic history without abandoning his earlier claim that history is the locus of revelation.

Scotus supplies the doctrine of the radical/absolute contingency of creation, the primacy of the will / posse esse, haecceitas and the claim that time is itself contingently instituted with creation and could have been otherwise. That gives the theological grammar for an open, future-oriented, eschatologically verifiable temporality rather than a necessary/Hegelian unfolding, and the foundation for the “contingent concept of time” the question names.

The disagreement is the second interlocutor.

Scotus + Heidegger cluster – now the majority in round 1. Colleagues 10,13,14,15,16,17,2,21,3,5,7,9 argue Heidegger supplies the phenomenological-hermeneutic articulation of that contingency. Pannenberg appropriates Being and Time’s analysis of temporality as ecstatic, futural, thrown-projection, historically disclosed and non-absolute, and transposes it from Dasein to being as such. That Heideggerian de-anthropologisation of time as horizon of happening rather than Newtonian container is what lets the artificial partition between “natural history” and “human history” collapse, and makes human history a particular instance of one contingent cosmic becoming. Scotus = modal contingency; Heidegger = ecstatic, relational temporality that makes a physics-engaged, non-anthropocentric cosmic history thinkable.

Scotus + Schelling cluster – still a substantial minority, Colleagues 1,11,12,18,19,20,4,6,8. They stress that the specific historic-philosophical warrant for eschewing artificial distinctions between types of history and the claim that human history has no intrinsic cosmic privilege is Schellingian. Friedrich Schelling’s Naturphilosophie / Ages of the World treats nature as primordial processual history in its own right, and nature and spirit as one unfolding cosmic process. Schelling provides the non-anthropocentric nature-as-history model that lets Pannenberg reinterpret rather than abandon his theology of history. Scotus provides contingent temporality; Schelling provides the cosmic-historical, de-anthropocentric historiography.

Key tensions noted across rounds: Heidegger gives the explicit phenomenological description of contingent, relational, future-open time needed for engagement with Einsteinian physics and for dissolving history types; Schelling gives the classic German Idealist precedent for nature-as-history and de-centering the human, but is perceived by the Heidegger camp as still necessitarian/teleological and less suited to the contingent-time claim. Unresolved: whether Pannenberg’s explicit historic citations for the de-anthropocentrization of history are Schellingian enough to outweigh Heidegger’s role in the description of temporality that the question foregrounds. The contingent concept of time is secure as Scotus; the second name remains contested between Heidegger for the phenomenology of ecstatic temporality and Schelling for the nature-as-history / non-privileged human history move. 1.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: T. John Duns Scotus and Friedrich Schelling

The late cosmic re-reading is a re-interpretation, not an abandonment, of the theology of history. The continuity is secured by a metaphysics of contingency for time itself and by a non-anthropocentric model of nature as history.

The contingent concept of time on which the whole cosmic model is built is Scotist. Pannenberg retrieves John Duns Scotus against an Augustinian-Thomist necessitarian picture of time and creation. Scotus’ doctrine of the absolute contingency of creation, the primacy of the will/posse esse and the claim that time is freely instituted with creation and could have been otherwise gives Pannenberg the theological grammar for a temporality that is not a necessary container, is genuinely open to the future and eschatologically verifiable, and for a cosmic history that is not teleologically necessitated.

The de-anthropocentrization of history, the eschewal of artificial distinctions between types of history and the claim that there is no principled ontological reason to privilege human history over other histories is Schellingian. Friedrich Schelling’s Naturphilosophie and late philosophy of nature/Ages of the World treats nature not as a static backdrop for spirit but as a primordial, processual history in its own right. Nature and spirit belong to one unfolding cosmic process. That is the explicit historic philosophical resource Pannenberg uses to re-situate human history as one history among histories within a single cosmic history and to argue that human history has no intrinsic cosmic priority.

Scotus supplies the modal contingency of creation and time; Schelling supplies the nature-as-history, non-anthropocentric historicity that lets Pannenberg dissolve the modern human/natural history split without abandoning the historicist structure of his earlier work. Heideggerian phenomenology of temporality is an important background descriptive resource for Pannenberg, but the two historic philosophical-theological pillars he explicitly invokes for the contingent-time cosmic history and for the rejection of a privileged human history are Duns Scotus for contingency and Schelling for cosmic historicity.

2.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: Y. John Duns Scotus and Martin Heidegger

The Scotist anchor is now the common ground, and rightly so. Pannenberg needs a metaphysics in which time and creation are not Augustinian-Thomist necessities but freely instituted and genuinely open. That is the Duns Scotus move: the radical contingency of creation, the primacy of the will, posse esse, and the possibility that time itself begins with creation and could have been otherwise. It is Scotus that gives Pannenberg the theological grammar for a contingent concept of time, an open future, and a cosmic history that is not teleologically necessitated.

What is being contested is the second partner, and here the physics-engaged reinterpretation points to Heidegger, not Schelling as the explicit temporal-ontological articulation.

The problem Pannenberg is trying to solve in the later work is not simply that nature is processual. It is how to dissolve the modern artificial partition between natural history and human history by re-describing time itself so that an Einsteinian, relational, non-absolute time becomes theologically intelligible. That re-description is Heideggerian.

Pannenberg takes up Being and Time’s analysis of temporality as ecstatic, futural, finite and historically disclosed — time as the horizon of happening rather than a neutral Newtonian container — and transposes it from Dasein to being as such. Once time is understood as thrown-projection, being-towards, the ecstatic unity of past-present-future, the ontological basis for a privileged human history disappears. Human history becomes a particular instance of a more primordial cosmic temporality, and there is no principled reason to hold human history as of more cosmic interest than other histories.

Schelling’s Naturphilosophie is important background for the German Idealist desire to think nature as process and to de-anthropocentrize historiography. That is why Schelling keeps appearing in the discussion. But Schelling remains in a German Idealist idiom of unfolding and identity that carries necessitarian, teleological baggage. He gives a nature-as-history image, not the phenomenological-hermeneutic account of contingent, ecstatic, future-open temporality that Pannenberg needs to make modern cosmology theologically readable.

In the later physics-informed model, Scotus supplies the modal contingency of creation and of time itself, and Heidegger supplies the description of that time as open, relational and eschatologically directed, which is what lets Pannenberg universalise historicity and argue for a single, contingent cosmic history without abandoning his earlier claim that history is the locus of revelation.

4.text:
**T. John Duns Scotus and Friedrich Schelling**

The later physics-engaged re-reading of the theology of history is presented by Pannenberg as a re-interpretation and a universalisation, not an abandonment, of the earlier eschatological historiography.

* The modal-temporal moment is Scotist. Against the Augustinian-Thomist necessitarian picture of time and creation, Pannenberg retrieves John Duns Scotus’ doctrine of the absolute contingency of creation, the primacy of the will, posse esse and the free institution of time with creation. Scotus gives the theological grammar of a time that is itself contingent, non-absolute, genuinely open to the future and could have been otherwise. It is that Scotist contingency of being and of time that makes a cosmic history possible which is open-ended, not teleologically necessitated in a Hegelian sense, and which remains eschatologically verifiable. That is the contingent concept of time on which the whole cosmic-history model is built.

* The historiographical, de-anthropocentrizing moment is Schellingian. The claim that the artificial modern distinctions between kinds of history are to be eschewed, that nature is not a static backdrop for spirit, and that there is no principled ontological reason to privilege human history over other histories, is the Naturphilosophie thesis. Friedrich Schelling’s *Naturphilosophie* and the late philosophy of the Ages of the World treat nature as a primordial, processual history in its own right and hold nature and spirit to belong to one unfolding cosmic process. That is the historic resource Pannenberg uses to re-situate human history as one history among histories within a single, non-anthropocentric cosmic history and to argue that human history has no intrinsic cosmic priority.

Scotus supplies the contingent temporality; Schelling supplies the nature-as-history, non-anthropocentric historicity that lets Pannenberg reinterpret rather than abandon his earlier claim to history. Heideggerian phenomenology of temporality remains an important background for Pannenberg’s discussion of time, but the historic philosophical-theological pillars explicitly invoked for the contingent-time model of cosmic history and for the dissolution of the human/natural history divide are Scotus for contingency and Schelling for cosmic historicity.

3.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: Y. John Duns Scotus and Martin Heidegger

Scotus is now unanimous as the modal-theological source for the contingent concept of time on which the late cosmic model is built. Pannenberg repeatedly retrieves John Duns Scotus against an Augustinian-Thomist necessitarian picture of time and creation: the radical contingency of creation ex nihilo, the primacy of the will/posse esse, haecceitas, a time that is itself freely instituted with creation and could have been otherwise, a beginning of time and a formally open future. That Scotist grammar is what gives the late work a theologically warranted open, non-necessitated, eschatologically verifiable temporality instead of a Hegelian necessary dialectic.

The second required pillar is the phenomenological articulation of that contingency as temporality itself and the dissolution of the modern partition between kinds of history. That is the Heideggerian moment. Pannenberg takes up Heidegger’s analysis of temporality in *Sein und Zeit* – time as ecstatic, futural, thrown-projection, being-towards, historicity as hermeneutic horizon rather than an absolute Newtonian container – and transposes it from Dasein to being as such. Once time is understood as an ecstatic, relational, horizon-constituting historicity rather than absolute succession, the modern artificial division between “natural history” and “human history” loses its ontological basis. Human history is de-centred and becomes one instance of a more primordial cosmic temporality; there is no principled reason to privilege human history over the history of the cosmos.

That Heideggerian de-anthropologisation of time as horizon of happening rather than Newtonian container is what lets the artificial partition between natural and human history collapse, makes human history a particular instance of one contingent cosmic becoming, and makes Einsteinian relational time theologically readable. reflection_text.3:

John Duns Scotus is unanimous as the historic theological source for the contingency of creation/time. Pannenberg repeatedly retrieves Scotus against Augustinian-Thomist necessitarianism: radical contingency of the world, primacy of the will/posse esse, haecceitas, creation ex nihilo, time itself contingently instituted with creation, a beginning of time, an open future. Scotus supplies the modal-ontological grammar for a time that could have been otherwise, is not an absolute Newtonian container, and can bear an eschatologically verifiable but non-necessitated cosmic process.

Disagreement on the second historic interlocutor persists but the balance has shifted strongly toward Scotus + Martin Heidegger in round 2.

Scotus + Heidegger bloc ~16 of 21 responses in this round, up from a majority already in round 0. Argument: the core problem in the late work is a reinterpretation of time itself. Pannenberg transposes Heidegger’s existential analytic of temporality in Being and Time – ecstatic, futural, thrown-projection, being-towards-death, historicity as hermeneutic horizon rather than absolute succession – from Dasein to being as such. Heidegger de-anthropologises/de-metaphysicises time, provides the phenomenological description of time as relational, non-absolute, future-open and eschatologically directed, which lets him read Einsteinian relational physics theologically and dissolve the artificial distinction between kinds of history. Scotus gives modal contingency, Heidegger gives the temporal articulation that makes a non-anthropocentric, single contingent cosmic history thinkable. Schelling is acknowledged as background for a non-anthropocentric intuition but not as the explicit source for the contingent concept of time; Heidegger’s critique of metaphysical time and ecstatic futurity is said to be what is required for a contingent, post-Newtonian temporality.

Scotus + Friedrich Schelling bloc ~5 responses in this round, persistent minority. Argument: contingency is Scotist, but the explicit historic philosophical scaffolding for eschewing artificial distinctions between types of history and denying a privileged cosmic status to human history is Schellingian. Schelling’s Naturphilosophie, Ages of the World and late philosophy of nature provide the model of nature as primordial processual history in its own right, of spirit and nature as one unfolding cosmic process, and the classic precedent for refusing an anthropocentric history. Scotus supplies the contingent temporality; Schelling supplies the non-anthropocentric nature-as-history model that lets Pannenberg reinterpret rather than abandon his earlier theology of history. Heidegger is described as phenomenological background, useful for description of temporality, but the two historic-theological pillars Pannenberg foregrounds for the cosmic-history claim are Scotus and Schelling.

Secondary positions noted earlier – Hegel+Schelling, Leibniz+Heidegger – are now marginal. Leibniz is invoked for relational anti-Newtonian time, Hegel for the historicist structure Pannenberg preserves, but they are not presented as the primary pairing for the contingent-time model.

The question explicitly foregrounds “a model of cosmic history that is built upon a contingent concept of time” and “eschewing the artificial distinctions between types of history”. The Heidegger reading stresses the contingent concept of time and the de-anthropologisation of time as horizon; the Schelling reading stresses the dissolution of human/natural history divide and the nature-as-history model. With the round-2 majority, the working hypothesis is Scotus for contingency and Heidegger for the temporal-hermeneutic articulation that makes the single, non-anthropocentric cosmic history possible, with Schelling remaining important German Idealist background but not the second explicit pillar Pannenberg mobilises for the physics-informed contingent-time argument.

The wording of the question foregrounding “eschewing artificial distinctions between types of history… no real reason to hold human history as of more cosmic interest than other histories” maps directly onto the Schellingian nature-as-history claim, while the Heidegger camp argues that claim is delivered via de-anthropologisation of time itself.

8.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: Y. John Duns Scotus and Martin Heidegger

The late physics-engaged re-description is a universalisation, not an abandonment, of Pannenberg’s theology of history. Human history is de-centred and re-situated as one historicity within a single contingent cosmic becoming and the modern artificial partition between natural and human kinds of history is dissolved. That move requires both a modal warrant for genuinely open time and a phenomenological description of temporality that can be de-anthropologised.

The modal warrant is Scotist and non-negotiable. Against the Augustinian-Thomist necessitarian picture of time and creation Pannenberg repeatedly retrieves John Duns Scotus: the radical/absolute contingency of creation ex nihilo, the primacy of the will/posse esse/haecceitas, the free institution of time with creation, the possibility that time could have been otherwise, a beginning of time with creation and a formally open future. That is the theological grammar for a contingent concept of time, for a temporality that is relational not absolute, and for a cosmic history that is eschatologically verifiable rather than teleologically necessitated.

The phenomenological-hermeneutic articulation of that contingency is Heideggerian. Pannenberg takes up Heidegger’s analysis of temporality in Sein und Zeit – time as ecstatic, futural, thrown-projection, being-towards, the horizon of historicity rather than a neutral Newtonian container – and transposes it from Dasein to being as such. Once time is understood as ecstatic-historical and future-directed, the ontological basis for the modern distinction between types of history collapses. Human history becomes a particular instance of one primordial cosmic temporality; there is no principled ontological reason to privilege human history over the history of the cosmos.

Scotus supplies the contingent ontology of creation/time; Heidegger supplies the de-anthropologised, ecstatic description of temporality that makes a single, non-anthropocentric cosmic history thinkable and lets Pannenberg eschew artificial distinctions between types of history while keeping the historicist-eschatological structure. Schelling’s Naturphilosophie provides important German Idealist background for the nature-as-history intuition, but the explicit conceptual work on a contingent, relational, future-open temporality adequate to modern physics is the Scotus–Heidegger pairing.

2.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: Y. John Duns Scotus and Martin Heidegger

Scotus is the fixed modal ground, and the discussion is now essentially unanimous on that point. Pannenberg needs a metaphysics in which creation and time are not Augustinian-Thomist necessities but freely instituted and genuinely open. That is the repeated retrieval of John Duns Scotus: absolute contingency of creation, primacy of the will and posse esse, time beginning with creation and being able to have been otherwise, a future that is formally open rather than teleologically necessitated. Without that Scotist grammar there is no theological warrant for a contingent concept of time and for a cosmic history that is eschatologically verifiable rather than dialectically necessary.

The second pillar is what makes that contingency operative as temporality in the late, physics-engaged reinterpretation. The question is not simply whether nature is processual, it is how Pannenberg can de-anthropologise time itself, dissolve the modern partition between natural history and human history, and read Einsteinian relational time theologically without abandoning his historicist structure.

That work is Heideggerian. Pannenberg takes up Heidegger’s analysis of temporality in Sein und Zeit – time as ecstatic, futural, thrown-projection, the horizon of historicity rather than a neutral Newtonian container – and transposes it from Dasein to being as such. Once time is understood as ecstatic-historical, finite and future-directed, the ontological basis for privileging human history disappears. Human history becomes a particular instance of one contingent, temporally structured cosmic becoming whose meaning is only complete eschatologically. It is that de-anthropologisation of time itself that lets Pannenberg eschew artificial distinctions between types of history and say there is no principled reason to hold human history as of more cosmic interest than other histories.

Schelling’s Naturphilosophie is real German Idealist background for the non-anthropocentric intuition that nature is history in its own right, and Pannenberg certainly inherits that impulse. 3.text:
Y. John Duns Scotus and Martin Heidegger

The late physics-engaged re-reading is a universalisation / radicalisation of the earlier theology of history, not an abandonment of it. The continuity is secured by a modal metaphysics of a genuinely contingent time and by a phenomenological-hermeneutic description of temporality that can be de-anthropologised and extended from Dasein to being as such.

The modal ground is Scotist and non-negotiable. Pannenberg retrieves John Duns Scotus against the Augustinian-Thomist necessitarian picture of time and creation: absolute/radical contingency of creation ex nihilo, primacy of the will / posse esse, haecceitas, time freely instituted with creation and therefore beginning with creation and could have been otherwise, and a formally open future. That gives the theological grammar for a contingent concept of time, for a temporality that is not an absolute Newtonian container, and for a cosmic history that is eschatologically verifiable rather than teleologically necessitated in a Hegelian sense.

The second, temporal-horizonal articulation is Heideggerian. Pannenberg takes up Heidegger’s analysis of temporality in Sein und Zeit – time as ecstatic, futural, thrown-projection, being-towards, the hermeneutic horizon of historicity rather than a neutral absolute succession – and transposes it from Dasein to being as such. Once time is understood as ecstatic-historical and relationally constituted, the modern artificial partition between natural history and human history loses its ontological basis. Human history is de-centred and becomes one instance of one primordial cosmic temporality; there is no principled ontological reason to hold human history as of more cosmic interest than other histories.

Scotus supplies the contingent ontology of creation/time; Heidegger supplies the de-anthropologised, ecstatic description of temporality that lets Pannenberg eschew artificial distinctions between types of history, read Einsteinian relational cosmology theologically, and present the move as a reinterpretation / universalisation of his earlier claim to history. Schelling’s Naturphilosophie remains important German Idealist background for the non-anthropocentric intuition that nature is processual, but the explicit conceptual work on a contingent, non-absolute, future-open temporality required for the physics-informed model is Scotist contingency articulated through Heideggerian temporality.

**Y. John Duns Scotus and Martin Heidegger**

The late physics-engaged re-description is a universalisation / re-interpretation of Pannenberg’s earlier eschatological theology of history, not its abandonment. Human history is de-centred and re-situated as one instance of one primordial cosmic temporality; the modern artificial partition between natural history and human history is dissolved and there is no principled ontological reason to privilege human history cosmically. That move requires both a modal metaphysics of genuinely contingent time and a phenomenological description of temporality that can be de-anthropologised and read with relativistic cosmology.

The modal ground is Scotist and non-negotiable. Against the Augustinian-Thomist necessitarian picture of time and creation Pannenberg repeatedly retrieves John Duns Scotus: the absolute/radical contingency of creation ex nihilo, the primacy of the will / posse esse / haecceitas, time freely instituted with creation and so able to have been otherwise, a genuine beginning of time with creation and a formally open future. Scotus gives the theological grammar for a contingent concept of time that is not an absolute Newtonian container, is relational, genuinely open-ended and eschatologically verifiable rather than teleologically necessitated in a Hegelian sense. It is that Scotist contingency which makes a cosmic history built on a contingent concept of time possible and secures continuity with the earlier historicist structure.

The phenomenological-hermeneutic articulation of that contingency is Heideggerian. Pannenberg takes up Heidegger’s analysis of temporality in *Sein und Zeit* — time as ecstatic, futural, thrown-projection, being-towards, the hermeneutic horizon of historicity rather than a neutral absolute container — and transposes it from Dasein to being as such.
